strengths: Novel BEV-based radar representation elegantly enables diffusion-based generation while preserving radar-specific attributes (RCS, Doppler) and maintaining computational efficiency compared to direct 3D approaches

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation framework with radar-specific metrics (Chamfer Distance, Density Similarity, Radar Attribute Fidelity, MMD) that properly assess geometric and distributional qualities beyond visual assessment

Strong experimental results with RadarGen substantially outperforming the RGB2Point baseline across nearly all metrics on MAN TruckScenes, with convincing qualitative visualizations showing well-aligned point clouds

Practical applicability demonstrated through three concrete applications: scene editing with plausible results, compatibility with downstream detectors achieving 66% detection rate on synthetic data, and data augmentation potential

Thorough technical exposition with clear mathematical formulation, justified design choices (e.g., LASSO deconvolution for sparse recovery), and comprehensive supplementary material with implementation details, ablation studies, and additional qualitative results

Honest and transparent acknowledgment of limitations including performance dependency on upstream models, struggles in low-light scenarios, and potential hallucinations in occluded regions, which strengthens credibility

Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem in autonomous driving research—generating realistic radar data from cameras—filling a gap between physics-based simulation and data-driven approaches
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to single dataset (MAN TruckScenes) without validation on other automotive radar benchmarks (nuScenes, Waymo, A2D2), limiting confidence in generalization to different vehicle configurations, sensor setups, or geographic regions

Significant acknowledged performance degradation in low-light scenarios with only limited qualitative analysis (Figure 12); no quantitative characterization of failure modes or performance across varying lighting conditions represents critical practical limitation for real-world autonomous driving

Fundamental dependency on high-quality upstream models (depth estimation, semantic segmentation) whose errors cascade into radar generation failures; impact of upstream model errors not thoroughly analyzed, particularly in challenging conditions

Limited methodological novelty as the core diffusion framework (SANA) and BEV representation are relatively straightforward applications of existing techniques; primary novelty lies in problem formulation and evaluation metrics rather than algorithmic innovation

Incomplete comparisons with related work—primary comparison against single RGB2Point baseline with no direct quantitative comparison with other radar simulation methods mentioned in related work (Song et al., Alkanni et al.) or physics-based simulators

Scene editing evaluation lacks quantitative rigor with only qualitative visual assessment; no metrics for editing quality, user studies, or evaluation of whether edited scenes produce realistic radar signatures in realistic scenarios

Computational cost analysis incomplete: 10.5 seconds inference per timestep on 8x L40 GPUs and 2-day training time stated without contextualization against alternative approaches or real-time feasibility assessment

Statistical rigor limited by lack of confidence intervals or significance testing; single train/test split (431 clips training, 49 clips evaluation) without exploration of sensitivity to random seeds or alternative splits makes result stability unclear

Detection compatibility evaluation narrow in scope, testing only single detector (VoxelNeXt) on 50m range scenarios; more comprehensive downstream task validation would strengthen practical applicability claims
